passages.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath; the plot begins
passages.happening: On another Sabbath, Jesus goes into the synagogue. A man with a withered, useless hand is there. Jesus' critics watch closely to see if he will heal on the Sabbath, so they can accuse him. Jesus calls the man to stand up in front of everyone. Then he asks them, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” They say nothing. Jesus looks around at them with anger and sorrow at their hard hearts, and tells the man to stretch out his hand. It is made whole. The Pharisees walk out and begin plotting with the Herodians how to kill him.
passages.hearers:
The man's life was not in danger. He could have waited one more day. That is exactly the critics' point: why not heal tomorrow? Jesus' question turns it around. To refuse to do good when you can is not neutral. It is a kind of harm.

The Herodians were people loyal to Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee who would later have John the Baptist killed. The Pharisees and the Herodians had little in common. The Pharisees wanted strict faithfulness to God's law. The Herodians backed a ruler who served Rome. For them to work together shows how threatening Jesus had become to both religious and political power.

Notice the irony. On the Sabbath, Jesus gives a man his hand back. On the same Sabbath, his opponents plan a death.
passages.ot: The law said the Sabbath was holy, a day for God (Exodus 20:8). The prophets also warned against keeping holy days while neglecting mercy. Jesus' question, ‘to save life or to destroy it’, asks what kind of day God's day is meant to be.
passages.hard: Mark says Jesus looked at them “with anger and sorrow.” Can Jesus be angry and still be good? Yes. His anger is not wounded pride. It is aimed at hearts so hard that they would rather keep a rule than see a man healed. And the anger is mixed with grief. This is anger that hurts for the people it is aimed at.
passages.asks: The critics watched Jesus closely, but only to catch him out. It is possible to study Jesus carefully and still refuse him. Ask whether you come to him to receive, or to judge.

passages.t: Crowds from every region and spirits silenced
passages.happening: Jesus withdraws to the lake with his disciples, and a huge crowd follows. They come from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and the area around Tyre and Sidon. The crush is so great that Jesus asks for a boat to be kept ready so he will not be squeezed. Sick people push forward to touch him. Unclean spirits fall down before him and shout, “You are the Son of God!” He sternly orders them not to make him known.
passages.hearers:
Mark's list of places is a rough map. Galilee is the north. Judea and Jerusalem are the south. Idumea lies further south still; it was the homeland of the family of Herod. ‘Beyond the Jordan’ is the land east of the river. Tyre and Sidon are cities on the coast to the north-west, outside the Jewish homeland. People are coming from every direction, Jewish and non-Jewish.

The boat was practical. On a beach packed with people, a boat a little way off shore gave Jesus room to speak and a way to leave.
passages.hard: Why silence the spirits when what they say is true? The demons are right about who Jesus is, but they are the wrong witnesses, and it is the wrong time. Jesus will not have his identity announced by evil, or made known before the cross shows what kind of Son of God he is. In Mark, the first human to say it plainly is a Roman soldier at the cross (15:39).
passages.asks: The crowd wants Jesus' power. The spirits know his name. Neither is the same as following him. Ask what draws you to Jesus: what he can do for you, or who he is.

passages.happening: Jesus goes up a mountain and calls the men he wants. He appoints twelve and calls them apostles, which means ‘sent ones’. They are to be with him, to be sent out to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons. Mark lists their names: Simon, whom Jesus names Peter; James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he calls Boanerges, ‘Sons of Thunder’; Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
passages.hearers:
Twelve was not a random number. Israel was made up of twelve tribes, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob. By choosing twelve, Jesus signals that he is gathering and renewing God's people.

Going up a mountain to do it would remind Jewish hearers of Moses, who met God on Mount Sinai and received the law that formed Israel as a people (Exodus 19).

The names are telling. Peter means ‘rock’. ‘Sons of Thunder’ suggests James and John had fiery tempers (see Luke 9:54). ‘Simon the Zealot’ translates an Aramaic word meaning ‘zealous’, used of people burning with zeal for God's law, and sometimes of those ready to fight Rome. In the same group sits Matthew, whom Matthew's Gospel calls a tax collector (Matthew 10:3). A man who might once have hated Rome and a man who had worked for its rulers are at the same table.
passages.ot: God told Israel at Sinai that they would be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). The twelve tribes were meant to show the nations what God is like. Jesus' twelve are the start of that people made new.
passages.hard: Why would Jesus choose Judas, knowing what he would do? Mark does not explain, and the list does not hide it: ‘who betrayed Him’ is written into Judas's name from the start. The Gospels show Jesus giving Judas the same calling, the same teaching, and the same place at the table as the rest. The betrayal was Judas's own choice, not a lack of welcome.
passages.asks: Notice the first purpose: ‘to accompany Him’, to be with him. The preaching and the power come after. Ask whether your service for God has grown faster than your time with him.

passages.t: Jesus' family thinks he is out of his mind
passages.happening: Jesus goes home, and the crowd gathers again until he and his disciples cannot even eat. When his family hears about this, they set out to take hold of him, because they are saying, “He is out of His mind.”
passages.hearers:
In Jesus' world, family honour mattered a great deal. A son who left his trade, drew huge crowds, clashed with religious leaders, and did not stop to eat could bring shame on the whole family. And the authorities were already plotting against him (3:6). His family may have been trying to protect him as much as to stop him.

This scene appears only in Mark. Matthew and Luke leave it out. It is the kind of detail early Christians would hardly have invented about Jesus' own family, which is one reason many scholars think it is an early memory.
passages.hard: Did Jesus' family really think he was mad? The Greek phrase in verse 21 is literally ‘those from him’ or ‘those around him’, and some have read it as his friends. But Mark soon brings in his mother and brothers (3:31), and most scholars take verse 21 as his family. Mark shows plainly that even those closest to Jesus did not yet understand him. Later his brother James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19). Misunderstanding was not the end of the story.
passages.asks: Following Jesus can look foolish even to the people who love us most. Ask whether you have let a family's or a friend's worry decide how far you will follow. Ask, too, whether you have been the worried family to someone else.

passages.t: The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man
passages.happening: Scribes who have come down from Jerusalem give their verdict: Jesus is possessed by Beelzebul, and he drives out demons by the power of the prince of demons. Jesus answers with short pictures. How can Satan drive out Satan? A kingdom or a house divided against itself cannot stand. No one can rob a strong man's house unless he first ties up the strong man. Then Jesus gives a solemn warning: every sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. He says this because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
passages.hearers:
The scribes from Jerusalem were the experts, sent from the religious centre. They cannot deny that Jesus drives out demons. So they explain where his power comes from: from the devil himself.

The name Beelzebul goes back to a Philistine god. In 2 Kings 1:2 a king of Israel sends to ask “Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.” Baal-zebub can mean ‘lord of the flies’, possibly a mocking change of the god's name. Many scholars think the original was Baal-zebul, ‘lord of the exalted house’ or ‘prince Baal’. By Jesus' day, Beelzebul had become a name for the chief of evil spirits.

If ‘zebul’ does mean house, Jesus' reply plays on it. The scribes call Satan the lord of the house. Jesus says he has come to tie up the owner and take back what was stolen.
passages.ot: The picture of the strong man comes from Isaiah. God asks, “Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?” and answers, “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved” (Isaiah 49:24-25). Jesus' healings and exorcisms are that rescue in action. The people held by evil are the plunder he is taking back.
passages.hard: What is the sin that will never be forgiven? In Mark, it is defined by the setting: the scribes were saying Jesus had an unclean spirit (3:30). They looked at the plain work of God's Spirit, setting people free, and called it the work of the devil. It is not a careless word spoken once in anger. It is a settled refusal to see God's goodness as good, a refusal that shuts the door on the very forgiveness Jesus offers. Many Christians have feared they committed this sin. A long pastoral tradition answers that the fear itself is a sign that the heart has not turned hard in this way. Note too what comes first: “the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies” (3:28). The promise is wide before the warning is given.
passages.asks: The scribes saw the same miracles as the crowd and drew the opposite conclusion. Evidence alone does not change a heart that has already decided. Ask whether there is anything God is doing that you have refused to call good, because of where it came from or who it came through.

passages.happening: Jesus' mother and brothers arrive and stand outside. They send word in to call him. The crowd sitting around him says, “Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You.” Jesus asks, “Who are My mother and My brothers?” He looks at the people sitting in a circle around him and says, “Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.”
passages.hearers:
In a culture where family was everything, these words would have landed hard. Family gave a person a name, a living, protection, and a place. To call strangers his mother and brothers was to say that a new family was being formed, not by blood but by doing God's will.

The scene is set up with care. His family is ‘outside’. The listeners are ‘around him’, in a circle. Mark has placed this right after the scribes' accusation, so the reader sees three groups: the critics who reject him, the family who misunderstand him, and the people sitting at his feet.

Jesus is not rejecting his mother. In John's Gospel he provides for her from the cross (John 19:26-27). He is opening the family to everyone who will listen and obey.
passages.hard: Who were Jesus' brothers? Mark 6:3 names four of them, James, Joses, Judas, and Simon, and mentions sisters too. Christians have understood this in different ways. Many Protestants take them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus. The Orthodox tradition has often taken them as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, and the Roman Catholic tradition as cousins or close relatives. The Greek word for brother can be used for close kin. This is a question on which faithful Christians differ, and the chapter's notes below set out the views.
passages.asks: Jesus counts as family everyone who does God's will, and he names sisters as well as brothers. Ask who sits in that circle with you, and whether the church you belong to feels like family. Ask, too, whether you are sitting inside, listening, or standing outside, asking him to come out to you.
